newsitem.title: LEBANON: World Bank chief backs Hariri in debt dispute.
newsitem.headline: World Bank chief backs Hariri in debt dispute.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn threw his support behind Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri in a public debate over Lebanon's ballooning public debt, saying he would act just like Hariri if he were running the country.
Wolfensohn said that even though he was concerned about the high level of Lebanon's debt he trusted the "financial good sense" of Hariri's government.

His remarks at a news conference in Beirut on Sunday night followed an outspoken call last week by Francois Bassil, president of the Lebanese Banks Association, for Hariri to curb the debt and lower interest rates to get the economy moving.

Bassil said the government's massive budget deficits and the mounting public debt were endangering everything Hariri had achieved in the past four years in his multi-billion dollar drive to rebuild Lebanon.

However, Wolfensohn said in response to a question at the news conference that he believed it was necessary to act fast and take risks when a country was emerging from a conflict like Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war.

"It seems to me that when you're trying to do a lot very quickly after a conflict you either have a choice of meeting peacetime standards or possibly taking risks in order to get things moving," he said.
"It seems to me that if I were in the shoes of the prime minister I would try and move quickly but have the diligence I know that he and the finance minister (Fouad Siniora) bring to it."
Wolfensohn, on the first visit by a World Bank chief to Lebanon, announced the bank had quadrupled its annual allocations to the country to more than $400 million from about $100 million.
He said the bank had "great confidence" in Lebanon "because right through the period of conflict, even when the central bank was being bombed, we were being paid.
"Until proven otherwise, it's my judgment that you can trust the financial good sense of this administration," he said.
"Of course, we are concerned about the high levels of debt but I am sure the government is more concerned than we are, so I'm prepared to leave it in their hands to worry about," he added.

Lebanon's debt has more than tripled since December 1993 from nearly 5 trillion Lebanese pounds to 17.5 trillion ($11.4 billion) at the end of March. This is nearly 83 percent of the estimated GDP of $13.9 billion at end 1996.
This year's target of a 36 percent deficit of government income against expenditure set in the budget law is being massively succeeded since the deficit reached 60.2 percent in May.
